definitions.definition: A rule of physics that says things naturally go from order to disorder over time.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle, but a puddle never freezes into an ice cube by itself.

definitions.definition: Something that stays the same no matter how you look at it or change the situation.
definitions.example: The number 2 is always 2, whether you're counting apples or stars.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'reason,' used in the Bible to describe God's eternal logic and order behind everything.
definitions.example: In John 1:1, 'the Word' is the Logos, the divine logic that created and holds the universe together.

definitions.definition: The idea that physical reality comes from information, not the other way around.
definitions.example: Like how a computer program creates a virtual world from code, the universe might be built from information.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to become more disordered over time.
definitions.example: A messy room gets messier on its own, but it takes work to clean it up.

definitions.definition: Rules in physics that say certain things (like energy or momentum) stay the same in a closed system.
definitions.example: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

definitions.definition: A math principle that says every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law.
definitions.example: Because the laws of physics are the same everywhere, energy is conserved.

definitions.definition: The idea that reality comes from information, and that information gets its meaning and direction from God's eternal logic (the Logos).
definitions.example: It's like saying a story comes from words, and the words get their meaning from the author's intention.

definitions.definition: Something that doesn't depend on anything else for its existence or truth.
definitions.example: A mathematical truth like 2+2=4 is true no matter what, not because of any situation.

definitions.definition: Being true or real no matter what perspective or reference point you use.
definitions.example: The speed of light is the same whether you're standing still or moving fast.

definitions.definition: Something that cannot be proven or explained solely by other facts or rules.
definitions.example: The fact that kindness is good can't be proven just by looking at atoms and molecules.

definitions.definition: When a truth or rule works in many different areas, not just one.
definitions.example: The idea of fairness applies to games, school, and work, not just one situation.

definitions.definition: The opposite of entropy; a measure of order or organization that increases.
definitions.example: A living plant growing from a seed is negentropic—it creates order from disorder.

definitions.definition: When parts of a system are connected and work together in a stable, orderly way.
definitions.example: A choir singing in harmony has coherence; a crowd shouting randomly does not.

definitions.definition: When a system loses its order and connections, becoming more random and separate.
definitions.example: A sandcastle falling apart into loose sand is decoherence.

definitions.definition: A theory that all the information in a volume of space can be stored on its surface, like a hologram.
definitions.example: Like a 3D image stored on a flat sticker, the universe's info might be stored on its edge.

definitions.definition: A state that tends to break down or change because it's not the most orderly or stable arrangement.
definitions.example: A tower of blocks is thermodynamically unstable—it will fall over eventually.

definitions.definition: The natural tendency for things to become more disordered over time.
definitions.example: The entropic pressure on a sandcastle means it will slowly crumble.

definitions.definition: A strategy to control or change what people believe by spreading false or misleading information.
definitions.example: Spreading fake news to confuse voters is an information operation.

definitions.definition: Deliberate interference or distortion added to a message to make it harder to understand the truth.
definitions.example: Someone talking loudly while you're trying to hear a friend is adversarial noise.

definitions.definition: How accurately a message or information is received compared to how it was sent.
definitions.example: A clear phone call has high signal fidelity; a crackly one has low fidelity.

definitions.definition: The medium or pathway through which information is transmitted.
definitions.example: A radio wave is a channel for music; your ears are a channel for sound.

definitions.definition: Signal-to-noise ratio; a measure of how much useful information there is compared to random interference.
definitions.example: A high S/N means a clear message; a low S/N means it's hard to hear over static.

definitions.definition: Default Mode Network; a set of brain regions active when you're daydreaming or thinking about yourself.
definitions.example: When you're not focused on a task, your DMN is active, letting your mind wander.

definitions.definition: The fundamental basis or reason why something exists or is real.
definitions.example: Saying 'God created it' is an ontological grounding for why the universe exists.

definitions.definition: The exact opposite characteristics of something, especially of truth or goodness.
definitions.example: If truth is stable, the anti-property would be instability.
